figures.caption: Figure 2: Noisy RNNs trained to path-integrate can internally generate replay trajectories resembling lived experiences. (a) A noisy RNN learns to path-integrate: it estimates a signal s(t) from (nonlinear) observations of velocity s′(t). Without input, this RNN’s noise-driven activity r(t) samples from the time-series distribution of awake activity, one timestep at a time (“replay”). (b) Each internally-driven replay trajectory is a single sample from a time-series distribution with strict temporal dependencies: awake trajectories start and stop at certain positions in specific orders, and replay trajectories reproduce these temporal structures. (c) Our definition of replay as sampling is distinct from other definitions of neural sampling in which stochastic input-driven trajectories are used to gather samples to perform Monte Carlo inference on a static distribution without temporal dependencies (see Section 2.3).

Figure 3: Momentum complements adaptation by sustaining traversal across attractor basins. Decoded 2D replay trajectories from noisy RNNs trained on one of four spatial navigation tasks: T-maze, triangle, biased rat random walk, and unbiased rat random walk. Replay trajectories darken chronologically over time. For T-maze and triangle tasks, the mean (solid) and standard deviation (faint) are shown for each trajectory direction, whereas for the rat tasks many individual trajectories are shown. Standard dynamics (overdamped, λv = 1, ba = 0) reconstruct awake trajectories but stall at terminal attractors. Like in Figure 1, adaptation (ba > 0) destabilizes attractors, which encourages exploration but also makes trajectories undershoot their targets, while biologically plausible momentum via input differentiation (λv < 1) accelerates convergence to target attractors. When combined, momentum counteracts adaptation-induced drag, causing replay trajectories to quickly traverse their environment more than with either mechanism alone.

Figure 4: Momentum temporally compresses replay. We calculate how long it takes replay trajectories to reach their endpoints, relative to awake trajectories (blue = faster, red = slower). Biologically plausible momentum via input differentiation (λv < 1) not only shortens this reach time, but makes it smaller than that of awake paths, temporally compressing awake activity by up to 30%. We do not include unbiased rat trajectories because they do not have defined endpoints, but we do confirm in Section D that momentum quickens them. The same trends hold in RNNs with tanh nonlinearities (Figure 14) and non-plausible momentum (Figure 10).

Figure 6: On average, momentum increases exploration via regions visited. Another relevant aspect of exploration is transitions not present in awake activity. (a) Here we quantify these transitions via regions visited (r.v.). Each region is an area where every point is closest to the same endpoint. In our T-maze and triangle tasks, awake paths go from starting points to endpoints and stay there, visiting two regions total (starting and ending). Meanwhile, adaptation (ba > 0) can make replay paths visit multiple endpoints or re-visit earlier endpoints (r.v. ≥ 3). (b) With adaptation and momentum (λv < 1), replay paths might visit (i) more, (ii) fewer, or (iii) the same regions. (c) However, on average, momentum increases regions visited, thus increasing exploration. See Figures 16 and 12 for versions with tanh RNNs and non-plausible momentum.

Figure 10: Momentum temporally compresses replay in RNNs with non-plausible momentum. This is another version of Figure 4, but now with non-plausible momentum (see Section A.4). See Figure 14 for a version with plausible momentum in tanh RNNs.

Figure 14: Momentum temporally compresses replay in tanh RNNs. This is another version of Figure 4, but with tanh RNNs. See Figure 10 for a version with non-plausible momentum and ReLU RNNs. Notably, adaptation does not slow replay notably in tanh RNNs.
